newsitem.title: UK: Scientist-BSE may possibly be spread cow-to-cow.
newsitem.headline: Scientist-BSE may possibly be spread cow-to-cow.

text.p: A British scientist said on Wednesday there is a possibility that mad cow disease could be spread from one animal to another in a small number of cases.

Professor Roy Anderson of Oxford University's Department of Zoology told BBC television that transmission from cow to cow could be one explanation for figures showing that there is a bigger risk of catching the disease for cows in larger herds.

"One hypothesis is that there could be a small amount of horizontal transmission, another could be that in larger herds more artificial protein feed is used because they are stocked at high density," he said.

"We're not able to discriminate between the two at the moment but we can say via analysis that the level of this extra transmission is at such a low level that it will have no material influence on the future of the epidemic."

British scientists have already recognised that Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease, can be spread from mother to calf. But in a report released earlier this year they said they were not sure whether if happens in the womb or from cow's milk.

The European Union imposed a worldwide ban on British beef exports in March last year after the British government admitted a possible link between eating beef and developing Creuzfeldt-Jakob Disease, a brain disease that is fatal.
EU veterinary inspectors have insisted the countries process meat and bone meal at higher temperatures and for longer periods so as to kill the infectious agents of the disease.
At the EU summit in Florence last June, agreement was reached on phasing out the ban on British beef exports once EU experts were satisfied with measures Britain was to take to eradicate BSE.
